planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or early fall in well-drained soil; some direct sun helps bring out the blue-gray leaf tone.

directions: Glauca is an old European selection of English boxwood, documented since the mid-1800s, grown for foliage carrying a distinct blue-gray or glaucous cast rather than the typical dark green of common boxwood. It builds into a dense, rounded shrub at a slow, measured pace and holds its form well with only light annual shearing. Grown mainly in historic arboretum and specialty collections today, it offers a cooler-toned alternative to standard green boxwood for borders, low hedges, or mixed foundation plantings.
sources: American Boxwood Society — International Checklist of Cultivated Buxus

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil; tolerates firmer pruning than finer-leaved cultivars once established.

directions: Bullata is an old English boxwood selection, documented since the mid-1800s, named for its thick, rounded leaves with a puckered or blistered surface quite unlike the flat foliage of common boxwood. It grows into a substantial, vigorous shrub over many years and tolerates heavier pruning than finer-textured cultivars, making it suitable for large hedges or bold topiary forms. Its coarse, tactile leaf surface gives plantings an unusual textural accent valued in collector gardens and historic landscapes.
sources: American Boxwood Society — International Checklist of Cultivated Buxus

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in spring or fall; needs only light trimming to keep its naturally dense outline.

directions: Decussata is a long-documented English boxwood selection named for its leaves, which sit in tightly overlapping, crossed pairs along the stem rather than the looser spacing typical of common boxwood. This close leaf arrangement gives the shrub an especially dense, fine-grained surface that holds a crisp outline with only light trimming. It has long been grown in specialty and heritage boxwood collections rather than mainstream nurseries, suiting gardeners seeking an authentic old European form for detailed hedging or topiary.
sources: American Boxwood Society — International Checklist of Cultivated Buxus

common_name: Blue Cone Boxwood (Narrow Conical Blue-Toned English Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil; some direct sun helps intensify the blue-green foliage tone.

directions: Blue Cone is an English boxwood selection valued for its naturally narrow, upright, conical habit paired with foliage carrying a cool blue-green cast. It needs little corrective pruning to hold its tidy cone shape, though light shearing can tighten the outline further for formal use. The combination of a distinct silhouette and unusual foliage color makes it a useful accent for narrow spaces or repeated vertical plantings where a change from standard green columnar boxwood is wanted.
sources: American Boxwood Society — International Checklist of Cultivated Buxus

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; tolerates colder winters better than English boxwood types.

directions: Winter Beauty is a Korean boxwood selection, part of the same breeding stream that produced several other cold-hardy Buxus sinica var. insularis cultivars now grown across the northern United States and Canada. It forms a dense, rounded shrub with small leaves that hold better winter color than many English boxwood types in harsh climates. Its compact habit and reliable cold tolerance suit foundation plantings, low hedges, and mixed borders in regions where standard English boxwood struggles through winter.
sources: American Boxwood Society — International Checklist of Cultivated Buxus

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in a sheltered site; less cold-tolerant than English or Korean boxwood.

directions: Buxus balearica, the Balearic or Majorcan boxwood, is a distinct Mediterranean species native to the Balearic Islands and parts of North Africa and southern Europe, separate from the far more common Buxus sempervirens. It carries noticeably larger, glossier leaves than common boxwood and grows slowly into a substantial shrub or small tree over many years, tolerating full sun as readily as light shade. It is markedly less cold-hardy than English or Korean boxwood, withstanding only light frost, so it is best suited to warm-temperate and Mediterranean-climate gardens where its bold, strongly aromatic foliage can be used for large-scale hedging or specimen planting.
